newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lebanese refugee acquitted of arson in Luebeck.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese refugee acquitted of arson in Luebeck.

text.p: A court in the German port city of Luebeck acquitted a 21-year-old Lebanese refugee, Safwan Eid, on Monday of starting a fire 18 months ago in an asylum-seekers' hostel that killed 10 residents and injured 38.

The fire in January 1996 was the worst ever to hit a foreigners' home in Germany and raised fears at the time of a renewed wave of neo-Nazi attacks like one that swept the country after unification in 1990.

Eid, a civil war refugee who had lived in the hostel with his family for six years, was arrested shortly after the blaze at the Luebeck hostel on suspicion of trying to get revenge in a petty quarrel with another resident.

He was later charged with aggravated arson and causing bodily harm. But prosecutors in the nine-month trial took the unusual step of calling for his acquittal earlier this month saying there had been no proof of his guilt during the trial.
Presiding judge Judge Rolf Wilcken told the court the trial had not succeeded in proving Eid's guilt.

Eid had always protested his innocence. Members of his family in the courtroom cheered when they heard the verdict. Eid, who spent seven months in investigative custody, was awarded compensation by the court for his time in jail.
The fire killed six people from the former Zaire, a man from Benin, a Lebanese and a woman from Angola and her six-year-old daughter.

But although state prosecutors joined Eid's defence in calling for his acquittal, lawyers representing the family of some victims had insisted the Lebanese refugee was guilty and demanded a conviction.
After judge Wilcken read out the verdict, the mother of one of the victims swore at Eid in Arabic and collapsed in sobs.
Prosecutors had based their case on three words Eid allegedly told a first aid worker after he was rescued during the night of the blaze: "It was us".

Eid, however, told the court that what he really said was: "It was them -- they set the stairs on fire," repeating something his father had just told him and said it was obvious his father was talking about a neo-Nazi attack.
Anti-racist and left-wing groups had launched a campaign for Eid's release. They argued the fire was a neo-Nazi attack and the accused was a victim.
Eid's defence team argued that prosecutors did not properly investigate four youths, including a skinhead from a local far-right group, who were detained near the scene.
Three of the young men, driving a stolen car, had singed hair. But police accepted their alibis and released them.
